description: Christian teachings on life after death across denominations, and responses to the problem of evil.
content_html:
What Is Eschatology?

Eschatology is the study of “last things” — death, judgement, and what happens after death. For Christians, eschatology is not morbid speculation but a source of hope: the belief that death is not the end, and that God will ultimately bring justice and renewal. This starred spec point (1.6*) requires students to compare Christian eschatological beliefs with those of another religion.

Resurrection, Judgement, Heaven and Hell

Most Christian traditions teach that after death, humans face judgement, and then enter either heaven or hell. Heaven is described as eternal life in the presence of God — a state of perfect joy, peace and communion with God. Hell is described as eternal separation from God. The 39 Articles of Religion (the foundational Anglican confession of faith) affirm belief in the resurrection of the body and eternal life, but do not specify the precise nature of hell. Some Christians interpret hell as eternal conscious punishment; others see it as the final annihilation of the unrepentant; still others (universalists) believe God will ultimately save all people.

2 Corinthians 5:1–10 is a key passage for Edexcel: Paul writes that believers groan in their earthly “tent” (the body), longing for a “heavenly dwelling” made by God. He says “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each of us may receive what is due to us for the things done while in the body.” This passage affirms both resurrection (a new, permanent body from God) and judgement (accountability for earthly life).

Key Fact

Purgatory is the Catholic and some Orthodox teaching that souls who die in a state of imperfect holiness undergo purification before entering heaven. It is not a second chance for the unrepentant but a process of preparation for those who die in God’s grace. Most Protestant traditions (as reflected in the 39 Articles, Article XXII) reject purgatory as “a fond thing vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture.” This denominational divergence is directly tested in Edexcel’s question on eschatology.

This lesson’s spec point is starred (1.6*), meaning students are expected to compare Christian eschatology with another tradition — the most likely comparison in the exam is Islam or Catholic Christianity. Key comparisons: Both Christianity and Islam teach bodily resurrection, final judgement, heaven (Paradise/Jannah in Islam) and hell (Jahannam). Both affirm that what happens after death is determined by one’s response to God during earthly life. Divergence 1 — Purgatory: Catholic Christianity has a doctrine of purgatory; Islam has no direct equivalent, though some scholars discuss the barzakh (an intermediate state between death and resurrection) as a period of waiting rather than purification. Divergence 2 — Nature of salvation: Christianity teaches salvation through faith in Jesus Christ (Acts 4:8–12). Islam teaches submission (islam) to Allah, with the balance of one’s deeds assessed on the Day of Judgement; there is no equivalent to the Christian doctrine of atonement through Christ’s death. Divergence 3 — The Trinity: Christian descriptions of heaven involve the beatific vision (seeing God as he is, including the Trinity); Islamic paradise does not involve a Trinitarian concept of God.

The Problem of Evil and Suffering

If God is omnipotent (all-powerful) and benevolent (completely good and loving), why does evil and suffering exist? This is called the problem of evil. Philosophers argue: if God were truly omnipotent, he could prevent suffering; if God were truly benevolent, he would want to prevent it; yet suffering exists. This creates a logical tension for Christian belief in God.

Christians distinguish two kinds of suffering. Moral evil (also called moral suffering) is evil caused by free human choices — war, murder, cruelty, theft. Natural evil is suffering caused by natural events — earthquakes, diseases, floods. Both challenge belief in a good God, but in different ways. Moral evil raises questions about why God gave humans free will knowing they would misuse it. Natural evil raises questions about why God designed a world that produces suffering independently of human choice.

Key Fact

Psalm 103 responds to the problem of evil with a declaration of God’s compassion: “The Lord is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love.” Christians use this Psalm to argue that God’s love and care for the suffering is itself part of the answer to the problem — God does not stand aloof but suffers with humanity (especially revealed in the incarnation and crucifixion). Psalm 119 returns repeatedly to trusting God’s word even in affliction: “It was good for me to be afflicted so that I might learn your decrees” — suggesting that suffering has a spiritual purpose for the believer. The book of Job is a sustained biblical engagement with the problem: Job suffers catastrophically without deserving it, protests to God, and ultimately receives not an explanation but an encounter with God’s greatness.

Solutions to the Problem of Evil

Christians offer several responses to the problem of evil. The free will defence argues that God gave humans genuine freedom, which makes moral evil a human responsibility rather than God’s. A world with free will is considered better than a world of moral robots, even if free will is misused. This does not fully explain natural evil, however.

COMMON EXAM ERROR: Students frequently confuse these two theodicies. They are distinct and must not be attributed to the wrong thinker. Augustine (354–430 CE): Evil is the privation (absence) of good — it has no independent existence but is what happens when goodness is removed. The cause of evil is the misuse of free will, first by Satan, then by Adam and Eve (the Fall). This is the ‘free will theodicy’ or ‘Augustinian theodicy.’ Books: City of God, Confessions. Key contrast: creation was originally ‘very good’ (Genesis 1); evil entered through human sin. Augustine does NOT use the phrase ‘soul-making.’ Irenaeus (c.130–202 CE): Humans were created immature, made in the ‘image of God’ but not yet in his ‘likeness’ — they need to grow. Evil and suffering are the necessary conditions for moral and spiritual development. Modern development: John Hick (*Evil and the God of Love*, 1966) called this the ‘soul-making theodicy’ or the ‘vale of soul-making’. The world is not a paradise but a place where souls develop through facing challenges and suffering. Key contrast with Augustine: evil is not a consequence of a past Fall but a necessary feature for human growth. NEVER attribute ‘soul-making’ to Augustine.
exam_tip_html: The Augustinian/Irenaean/Hick distinction is one of the most commonly examined misconceptions in this topic. In the exam, if asked about the ‘vale of soul-making,’ name both Irenaeus (the originator) and John Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966) who developed it — do NOT attribute it to Augustine. For a 5-mark question requiring a source of wisdom, you can cite Psalm 103 (“The Lord is compassionate and gracious”), Psalm 119 (“It was good for me to be afflicted”), 2 Corinthians 5:1–10, or the 39 Articles by name. On 12-mark Discuss questions about whether suffering disproves God’s existence, the strongest answers develop both the intellectual challenge (the logical problem of evil) AND at least two responses (free will, soul-making, the cross as God’s solidarity with suffering), then weigh them explicitly before concluding. SPaG: spell ‘eschatology’, ‘omnipotent’, ‘benevolent’ and ‘theodicy’ correctly for those marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christian eschatology teaches resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell; Catholics add purgatory (rejected by Protestants via the 39 Articles); 2 Corinthians 5:1–10 affirms both resurrection and judgement. Comparison point: Islam also teaches resurrection and judgement but without purgatory or atonement through Christ.
  • The problem of evil asks how an omnipotent, benevolent God can allow moral suffering (caused by human choices) and natural suffering (earthquakes, disease); Psalm 103, Psalm 119 and Job are biblical responses showing compassion, trust and encounter with God.
  • Augustine: evil as privation of good caused by the Fall and free will. Irenaeus/John Hick: the ‘vale of soul-making’ — suffering is necessary for moral/spiritual development. Never attribute soul-making to Augustine.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- Christians believe in the resurrection of the body after death.
- Christians believe in a final judgement where each person faces accountability for their earthly life.
- Christians believe in heaven — eternal life in God's presence.
- Christians believe in hell — eternal separation from God.
- Catholic (and some Orthodox) Christians believe in purgatory — purification for souls not yet fully holy.
- Protestant traditions (39 Articles) reject purgatory.
Each point must be identifiably distinct — not three sentences rephrasing the same idea.

practice_questions.text: Describe what the 39 Articles of Religion teach about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- The 39 Articles affirm belief in the resurrection of the body.
- They affirm eternal life in heaven for the saved.
- Article XXII explicitly rejects purgatory as 'a fond thing vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture.'
- They reflect the Protestant (Anglican) position that heaven and hell are the only post-mortem destinations.
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the problem of evil challenges Christian belief in God.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Moral evil (caused by human choices — war, murder, cruelty) challenges belief in an omnipotent God: if God is all-powerful, why does he allow humans to choose to harm each other? Some conclude that either God is not all-powerful, or he does not care.
- Natural evil (earthquakes, disease, floods) challenges belief in a benevolent God: unlike moral evil, natural evil cannot be blamed on human free will. A truly loving God could apparently design a world without natural disasters. Its existence seems incompatible with a creator who is both powerful and good.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian responses to the problem of evil, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- The free will defence (Augustine): God gave humans genuine freedom; moral evil is the result of that freedom being misused. God is not responsible for choices made by free creatures. A world with free will is better than a world of moral robots, even if free will is misused.
- The soul-making theodicy (Irenaeus, developed by John Hick in Evil and the God of Love, 1966): suffering is the necessary condition for moral and spiritual growth. The world is a 'vale of soul-making' — if everything were comfortable, humans would never develop courage, compassion or faith. Psalm 119 reflects this: 'It was good for me to be afflicted so that I might learn your decrees.'

The 5th mark: name a source — 'John Hick, Evil and the God of Love (1966)', 'Psalm 103', 'Psalm 119', '2 Corinthians 5:1-10', or the book of Job. Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'The vale of soul-making is the most convincing Christian response to the problem of evil.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources (Hick, Augustine, scripture); explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- The soul-making theodicy explains both moral and natural evil: both are necessary conditions for humans to develop virtues like courage, compassion and faith. It is more comprehensive than the free will defence, which only addresses moral evil.
- John Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966) grounds soul-making in Irenaeus's theology (c.130-202 CE) — the idea that humans are created immature and grow towards 'the likeness of God.' This gives the theodicy deep roots in Christian tradition, not just modern philosophy.
- The Bible supports the idea that suffering has a developmental purpose: Psalm 119 states 'It was good for me to be afflicted'; the book of Job ends not with an explanation of Job's suffering but with his deepened encounter with God.

Arguments against:
- The soul-making theodicy struggles with extreme suffering (Holocaust, childhood cancer) that goes far beyond any plausible 'educational' purpose. John Hick himself acknowledged this weakness. A child who dies in agony before developing moral character cannot easily be said to have 'benefited' from suffering.
- Augustine's free will defence has strong scriptural grounding in the Fall narrative (Genesis 3) and Paul's teaching on original sin. For many Christians this is more convincing because it identifies a cause of evil (human rebellion) rather than asking victims to find meaning in their pain.
- Non-religious critics argue that both theodicies are post-hoc rationalisations — invented to protect belief in God rather than genuine explanations. The problem of evil, they argue, gives good reason to conclude there is no God.
- Both theodicies leave natural evil partially unexplained. If God could have made a world without earthquakes or disease but chose not to, soul-making does not fully answer why.

SPaG: 'theodicy', 'eschatology', 'omnipotent', 'benevolent' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two similarities between Christian and Islamic beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required. (This question addresses the comparison requirement of starred spec point 1.6*.)

Acceptable explanations:
- Both Christianity and Islam teach that after death all people will face judgement by God: Christians believe they will appear before 'the judgment seat of Christ' (2 Corinthians 5:10); Muslims believe their deeds will be weighed on the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din).
- Both Christianity and Islam teach that the outcome of judgement is either heaven or hell: Christians describe heaven as eternal life in God's presence; Islamic teaching describes Paradise (Jannah) as a state of joy and divine favour. Both traditions describe hell as a place of punishment for the unrepentant.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the 'vale of soul-making' theodicy?
options: Augustine's teaching that evil is the privation of good, caused by the Fall
The Catholic doctrine that souls are purified in purgatory before entering heaven
Irenaeus and John Hick's teaching that suffering is necessary for moral and spiritual development
The idea that God does not exist because suffering disproves his existence

knowledge_checks.q: The 39 Articles of Religion (Anglican) reject which afterlife doctrine as having 'no warranty of Scripture'?
In the Augustinian theodicy, evil is explained as the _____ of good — it has no independent existence but is what happens when goodness is removed.
The branch of theology dealing with death, judgement and the ultimate destiny of humanity is called _____.
Match each thinker or text to the response to suffering they represent:
right: Soul-making: evil is necessary for moral/spiritual development
Free will theodicy: evil entered through the Fall and misuse of free will
God is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger — a declaration of divine love amid suffering

flashcard_questions.a: The branch of theology concerned with death, judgement and the ultimate destiny of humanity.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 2 Corinthians 5:1-10 teach about life after death?
flashcard_questions.a: Believers receive a heavenly dwelling from God and face the judgement seat of Christ.

flashcard_questions.q: What is purgatory, and which major Christian tradition rejects it?
flashcard_questions.a: Catholic purification after death before heaven — rejected by Protestants (39 Articles, Article XXII).

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two types of evil or suffering distinguished in Christian theology?
flashcard_questions.a: Moral evil (caused by human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease).

flashcard_questions.q: What does Psalm 103 say about God in relation to suffering?
flashcard_questions.a: That the Lord is compassionate, gracious, slow to anger and abounding in love.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the book of Job illustrate about the problem of evil?
flashcard_questions.a: That innocent suffering exists; Job protests to God and receives an encounter with God's greatness, not an explanation.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Augustinian theodicy's explanation of evil?
flashcard_questions.a: Evil is the privation of good — caused by the Fall and the misuse of free will.

flashcard_questions.q: Who developed the 'soul-making' theodicy in modern form, and in which book?
flashcard_questions.a: John Hick, in Evil and the God of Love (1966).
Hick's term for the world as a place where moral and spiritual character develops through encountering suffering.

flashcard_questions.q: Augustine described the original state of creation as what, before the Fall?
flashcard_questions.a: Very good — as declared in Genesis 1; evil entered only through sin.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Irenaeus, whose theodicy John Hick developed, active?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 130-202 CE — an early Church Father.

glossary_terms.definition: From the Greek 'eschatos' meaning last — the branch of theology concerned with death, judgement and the ultimate destiny of humanity.
All-powerful — able to do anything that is logically possible.
Entirely good and loving, wanting only the best for creation.
The intellectual challenge posed by the existence of evil and suffering to belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God.
John Hick's development of Irenaeus's idea that the world is not a paradise but a vale of soul-making where humans develop moral and spiritual character through encountering suffering.
